lessons.title: Measuring turns

lead.text: Stand in the middle of a room and face a door. Turn until you face that door again and you have made a whole turn. Turn only until you face the opposite wall and you have made half of one, a half-turn. Stop when you face the wall on your left or right and you have made a quarter-turn.

These turns fit together neatly. Two quarter-turns make a half-turn, and four make a whole turn, whichever way you are facing when you start. Turns can also be added like lengths. A half-turn followed by another half-turn is a whole turn, and you are facing the door again.

Counting in quarter-turns is enough for the skater at the start of the lesson. It is too coarse for most jobs, though. A door that has swung open a little has made neither a quarter-turn nor a half-turn, and to describe that you need a scale with finer marks. First, the skater's problem.
Use the quarter-turn as your unit and count what she has made.

A finer scale cuts the whole turn into 360 equal small turns. Each one is called a degree and is written 1°, so a whole turn is 360° and a half-turn is half of that. The number 360 was chosen long ago because it divides evenly in so many ways, which lets you cut a turn into halves, quarters, fifths and many other equal parts.

Two straight lines that meet at a point leave a gap between them, and the size of that gap is an angle. The corner of this page is an angle, and so is the gap between the hands of a clock. We measure an angle by how much turning it takes to swing one line round onto the other, using degrees.
The corner of a page is a quarter of a whole turn. An angle like that is called a right angle. You already have what you need to find its size in degrees.
Use the size of a whole turn and the fraction of it that a right angle takes up.

A right angle measures 90°. Now cut one in two. Draw a line from the corner of a page out across the page, and the single right angle becomes two smaller angles side by side. Together they fill the corner exactly as before, so their sizes must add up to 90°.

That gives a way to find a missing angle with one subtraction. If you know the whole and one part, the other part is what remains. Say one part is 25°. The other is 90° − 25° = 65°. The figure shows two corners, each with one part marked. Switch between them and see how the leftover part changes.

afterFigure.text: The same reasoning works wherever a fixed amount of turn is shared between pieces. A corner is only the first case, with a total of 90°. The next case has a bigger total.

lead.text: Here is a corner with one part marked. The other part is the rest of the corner.

Turn through a half-turn and you finish facing the opposite way, so a half-turn is what a straight line looks like when you draw it. Its size is 180°. An angle of exactly that size is called a straight angle. Now split a straight angle by drawing a line out from a point on it. You get two angles side by side, and together they fill the straight line.

The idea from the corner carries over with a new total. Two angles on a straight line add up to 180°, so each one is 180° minus the other. If one is 120°, the other is 180° − 120° = 60°. The answer is smaller than the total, which makes a quick check: a part is never bigger than the whole it came from.

afterFigure.text: A straight line is half a turn. That leaves the other half still to come, and the full circle is the last case.

lead.text: Two angles share a straight line, and you know one of them.

steps.headline: All the way round a point

lead.text: Stand where several lines meet and look round you. The angles between neighbouring lines go all the way round the point and fill the whole turn. A whole turn is 360°, so the angles round a point add up to 360°.

The total also tells you how much turn is left on a dial. A pointer that has swung through 200° has 360° − 200° = 160° of its turn still to come. The figure shows the part already made and the part that remains. Together they fill the circle.
Every problem so far has worked the same way. Decide which total applies, 90° in a corner, 180° on a line or 360° round a point, then take away the parts you know.
A pointer sweeps round a dial, and part of its turn is already made.

One more point about angles before the check. Compare the minute hand of a clock on a church tower with the minute hand of a wristwatch. From 12 to 3 each hand turns through a right angle, although one is a metre long and the other a few millimetres.
The two lines that make an angle are called its arms. Drawing the arms longer makes the picture bigger and adds no turn, because the turn depends only on the directions the arms point.
So the size of an angle never depends on how long its arms are. That matters when you read a diagram, where a long arm can make one angle look larger than another even when the two match.
A diagram is redrawn with every line twice as long.

blocks.text: A skater glides onto the ice, faces the far end of the rink and spins on the spot. She makes half a turn, so she is looking back at the way she came in. Then she spins on for one more quarter-turn and stops.

She wants to finish facing the far end, as she did when she began, but she isn't sure how much further to spin. A coach at the barrier can tell her at once by counting how much of a turn she has made and how much is left.

Almost every shape has corners, and a corner is a turn. This lesson starts with the skater. It gives you a way to put a number on a turn, and then a quick way to find the missing part of a turn whenever the rest is known.

intro.promise: By the end you'll measure turns in degrees and find a missing angle in a corner, on a line and round a point.

recap.keyIdea: An angle measures a turn. Angles that fill a corner add to 90°, so a missing one is found by subtraction. A straight line and a full turn work the same way, with totals of 180° and 360°.

blocks.text: Back with the skater, you counted the quarter-turns she had made and found the one still to come. After that you put numbers on turns, and found a missing part each time by subtracting what you knew from the total.
You found 112° beside 68° on a line and 220° left of a full turn after 140°, and you saw that longer arms change nothing about the angle.

recap.nextHook: A straight line is a half-turn of 180°. Tear the three corners off a paper triangle and set them side by side, and they seem to fill that straight line exactly. The next lesson checks whether that always happens.

lessons.title: Angles in triangles

lead.text: The last lesson showed that a straight line is a half-turn of 180°. The torn corners of the paper triangle fit along such a line, so together they make a half-turn too. Each corner of a triangle is an angle, and the three angles of a triangle always add up to 180°. We call that total the angle sum of a triangle.

It holds for every triangle. A tall thin triangle has one very small angle and one very large one, and a wide flat triangle has a different mix. The total stays at 180° whatever the shape, because the torn corners would still lie flat along a line. The figure shows two different triangles with their three angles.

afterFigure.text: So if you know two of the corners, the total fixes the third. First, try it on the torn triangle.

lead.text: Lay the three torn corners side by side along a straight edge.

Because the three angles add up to 180°, a missing angle is whatever is left after the known ones are taken away. Add the two you know and take the sum away from 180°. For a triangle with angles of 62° and 41°, the two add to 103°. Taking that from 180° leaves 77°, which is the third angle.

A quick check is to add all three at the end. They should come to 180°, and here 62° + 41° + 77° = 180°. The method works on any triangle where you can see two of the angles, so the next question has a triangle with two angles marked.
Two angles of this triangle are marked. The third corner fills what is left of the 180°.
One kind of triangle comes up so often that it has a name. A triangle with one right angle, a corner of 90°, is called a right triangle. The corner of a set square is one.

The angle sum tells you something about the other two corners. The right angle uses up 90° of the 180°, so the other two share the remaining 90°. If one of them is 20°, the other is 90° − 20° = 70°. The figure shows two right triangles, and in each the two angles that are not the right angle add to 90°.
Right triangles come back later in the course whenever distances need measuring, so it is worth knowing how their angles behave.
Find the third angle by taking both known angles from the total.
Some triangles have two angles of the same size. When two angles are equal and you know the third, the method gets one extra step.

Take the known angle away from 180° first. What remains has to be shared between the two equal angles, so each gets half of it. If the odd angle is 40°, then 180° − 40° = 140° remains, and half of that is 70° for each of the equal pair. Check the result: 70° + 70° + 40° = 180°.
So far every triangle we have met was a real one. The last question is whether any three numbers can be the angles of a triangle.

cases.label: Two angles of 70° and one of 40°
Two angles of 55° and one of 70°

lead.text: The two equal angles share what the third angle leaves.

steps.headline: Which sets of angles are possible

lead.text: Any three positive numbers can be written down as angles, but only some sets are the corners of a real triangle. The test is the angle sum. If the three add up to exactly 180°, a triangle with those angles can be drawn. If they add up to more or to less, no triangle has those angles, because the torn corners would either run past the straight edge or leave a gap.

Angles of 30°, 60° and 90° can form a triangle, because they add to 180°. It is the right triangle again. Angles of 50°, 60° and 80° cannot, because they add to 190°. A corner with no turn is no corner at all, so every angle must also be greater than 0°.
Use that test on the next question.
A student wants to draw a triangle with two right angles. Test the angles against the total before drawing.

blocks.text: Cut a triangle out of paper. It can have any shape you like, tall and thin or short and wide. Tear off its three corners and lay them side by side on the table with their points touching.

The corners fit together along a straight edge, with no gap and no overlap. Try again with a different triangle and the same thing happens. In one triangle two of the corners measure 70° and 50°, and the third is too crumpled to measure.

It is odd that three corners of such different sizes should always fill a straight edge exactly. This lesson turns that fact into a tool. It gives you one rule that holds for every triangle, and a quick way to find a corner you cannot measure.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find a missing angle in any triangle and tell whether three angles could make one.

recap.keyIdea: The three angles of a triangle add to 180°, so any missing angle is 180° minus the others.

blocks.text: You found that corners of 70° and 50° leave 60° of the straight edge for the third. After that you used the same subtraction on a right triangle and on a triangle with two equal angles.
You also used the total to rule out a triangle with two right angles.

recap.nextHook: Corners are only one thing to measure on a shape. Next, a room needs skirting board along its edge and tiles across its floor, and the two jobs call for different numbers.

lessons.title: Boundary and area

lead.text: Take the tiling first. A tile is a square and every tile is the same size, so tiles laid edge to edge, with no gaps and no overlaps, cover a floor completely. The number of tiles it takes measures how much floor there is. That amount is called the area of the floor, and it is counted in unit squares. If each tile is 1 metre across, a tile is a square metre, written 1 m², and a floor that takes 12 tiles has an area of 12 m².

Counting tiles one at a time is slow. Tiles lie in rows, and every row has the same number of tiles. A floor with 4 rows of 8 tiles holds 8 + 8 + 8 + 8 = 32 tiles, which is 4 × 8. So the area of a rectangle is the number of rows times the number of tiles in each row, and that is the same as its length times its width.

afterFigure.text: The small 2 in m² records that the unit is a square with a metre along each side.

lead.text: Count with the rows, not one tile at a time.

Now the skirting board. It runs along the bottom of every wall, so the length you need is the distance all the way round the edge of the room. That distance is the perimeter of a shape. You find it by adding the lengths of all the sides, and it is measured in ordinary units of length such as metres.

A rectangle has a helpful pattern, because its opposite sides are equal. A room 9 m long and 3 m wide has two walls of 9 m and two walls of 3 m, so its perimeter is 9 + 3 + 9 + 3 = 24 m. You can shorten the sum to 2 × (9 + 3), which counts two lengths and two widths. Either way the unit is metres, since a perimeter is a distance.

afterFigure.text: The room now has a perimeter and an area, and both come from the same two numbers. Next, a 6 m by 4 m room needs both.

steps.headline: A room is 6 m by 4 m. Find its perimeter and its area.

workedSteps.text: Add all four sides for the skirting board.

lead.text: Perimeter and area both come from the same two sides, but they do not move together. Take two rooms that each need 16 m of skirting board. One is 4 m by 4 m. The other is a long strip, 7 m by 1 m.

Add the sides and each perimeter is 16 m: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 for the square and 7 + 1 + 7 + 1 for the strip. Now count tiles. The square has 4 rows of 4, which is 16 tiles. The strip has 1 row of 7, which is 7 tiles.

Both rooms have the same distance round them, yet the square takes more than twice as many tiles. Once the perimeter is fixed, the shape decides the area. The two measures answer different questions, and a number for one tells you little about the other.
Add up the sides round each rectangle, then count the squares inside it.

Many everyday problems come down to choosing between the two measures. A fence, a picture frame or a border runs along an edge, so each needs a perimeter. Paint, turf, carpet and tiles cover a surface, so each needs an area. Asking whether the job goes round the edge or across the inside settles it.

The unit shows which measure an answer is. A perimeter is a length, so it is written in units such as metres. An area counts squares, so it is written in square units such as m². Always write the unit with the answer, since a bare 24 could be either.
Count the squares row by row.

So far the sides have come first and the area second. A problem can run the other way. A tiler knows a floor takes 40 tiles and that one wall is 5 tiles long. The puzzle is the length of the other wall.

The area is the number of rows times the number of tiles in each row, so 40 = 5 × (the other side). Division undoes multiplying, and 40 ÷ 5 = 8, so the other wall is 8 tiles long. Whenever you know the area and one side of a rectangle, divide the area by that side to find the other.
One more idea needs both measures together: a fixed amount of fence and a choice of shape for the garden it surrounds.
Two lengths and two widths make 20 m of fence, so one length and one width add to 10 m. The sides must be whole numbers.

blocks.text: You have bought a flat with an empty rectangular room, and two jobs need doing. Skirting board has to run along the bottom of every wall, and the floor has to be tiled from wall to wall. The same room goes into both jobs, but they ask for different amounts.

The skirting board is sold by the metre, so you need a length: how far it is round the room. The tiles are sold by the box, so you need a count: how many fit on the floor. Two rooms can need the same length of skirting board and very different numbers of tiles.
This lesson takes the two jobs one at a time and then puts them side by side. By the end you can tell which measurement a problem is asking for and work out both for any rectangle.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell the distance round a rectangle from the space inside it, and find both.

recap.keyIdea: Perimeter is the distance round a shape and area counts the squares inside. For a rectangle, add all four sides for the first and multiply the two sides for the second.

blocks.text: Back in the room, you counted 15 tiles in 3 rows of 5 and then worked out the skirting board for rooms of different shapes.
You found that 6 by 4 and 8 by 2 rectangles share a perimeter but not an area, and that 20 m of fence can enclose up to 25 m².

recap.nextHook: Rectangles are easy to count in rows. A card cut corner to corner leaves two triangles with a slanting edge, and the next lesson works out which length to use for them.

lessons.title: Base and height

lead.text: A rectangle's area is its length times its width. A card 10 cm by 3 cm has an area of 30 cm². Cut it from one corner to the opposite corner and the two triangles that result are identical, so each one has half the card's area: 15 cm².

To talk about the triangle, give its sides names. The side it sits on is its base. The other length of the card, measured straight up from the base, is its height. The triangle's area is half of the base times the height, here ½ × 10 × 3 = 15 cm².

afterFigure.text: That works because this triangle came from a rectangle with square corners. Most triangles do not, and for them it is less clear which length plays the part of the height.

lead.text: Think about what the cut does to the card.

steps.headline: The height of a leaning triangle

lead.text: Now keep the same base and push the top corner to one side, so that the triangle leans. Its sloping edges are longer than the height used to be. The height is the straight distance from the top corner down to the line of the base, and it meets the base at a right angle. Because it meets the base at a right angle, it is called the perpendicular height.

Take a triangle with a base of 8 cm. Its top corner is 6 cm above the base line, and in the first picture the sloping edge is 10 cm long. The perpendicular height is 6 cm. The 10 cm edge is longer and it leans, so it is not the height.

afterFigure.text: Any side can be chosen as the base, provided the height is then measured from the opposite corner at a right angle to it. For now the flat edge stays at the bottom.

lead.text: Draw a rectangle round a leaning triangle, with the triangle's base as its bottom edge and its top corner touching the top edge. A line straight down from the top corner splits the picture into two parts. In each part the triangle fills exactly half of a rectangle, so over the whole picture the triangle fills half of the big rectangle.
That makes the area of a triangle half the base times the perpendicular height, whatever the lean. Compare the two cases in the figure. The base and height match, and so do the areas.
Slide the top corner along a line parallel to the base and the sloping sides change while the base and the height stay as they were. So the area stays as it was.
This triangle has a base and a perpendicular height. Picture the rectangle with the same base and height. The triangle covers half of it.
Slide the top corner sideways along a line parallel to the base. The sloping sides change length.

Join two copies of the same triangle along a sloping edge, with one of them turned upside down. The pair makes a four-sided shape whose opposite sides are parallel, which means they run side by side and never meet. A shape like that is a parallelogram. A rectangle is one with square corners, and most parallelograms lean.

The parallelogram has the triangle's base for its base and the same perpendicular height. Its area is two triangles' worth. Each triangle is ½ × base × height, so two together are base × height, because the half cancels. For a parallelogram with a base of 7 cm and a perpendicular height of 4 cm, the area is 7 × 4 = 28 cm².
The slanting side of a parallelogram does not enter the sum, any more than the sloping edge of a triangle does. Only the base and the perpendicular height count.
Treat the parallelogram as two matching triangles.

Sometimes the area is known and a length is missing. The area of a triangle is half of the base times the height, so base times height is twice the area. For a triangle with an area of 24 cm² and a base of 6 cm, base times height is 48. Divide by the base and the height is 48 ÷ 6 = 8 cm.

The steps run backwards: double the area to undo the halving, then divide by the base to undo the multiplying. A common slip is to divide the area by the base and stop, which gives only half the height. You can check any answer by running the formula forwards. Here ½ × 6 × 8 = 24, which matches.

afterFigure.text: That is every piece the lesson needs. The last question uses them in a new setting.

lead.text: You know the area and the base this time, not the height.

blocks.text: A rectangular card measures 6 cm by 4 cm. You cut it with a ruler and a craft knife, straight from one corner to the opposite corner. That leaves two pieces, and they match: turn one round and lay it on the other, and the edges line up.

Each piece is a triangle. A triangle has no tidy rows of squares like the tiles of the last lesson, because its sloping edge slices through them. The card still gives you a way in, because you already know how much card there was before the cut.

This lesson starts with the card and then changes the triangle step by step. We lean it, slide its top corner sideways and join two copies together. At each stop one length matters and another does not, and the lesson is learning which is which.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find a triangle's area from its base and perpendicular height, and use the same idea for a parallelogram.

recap.keyIdea: A triangle's area is half of base × perpendicular height, and a parallelogram's is base × perpendicular height.

blocks.text: Back at the card, each half of the 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle came to 12 cm². You then saw that sliding a triangle's top corner leaves its area alone, because only the base and the perpendicular height count.
You also found that a 30 m² flag with a 10 m base stands 6 m tall.

recap.nextHook: Real floors and fields are rarely a single rectangle or triangle. Next, a hall with a corner missing shows how to measure a shape by cutting a piece away or splitting it up.

lessons.title: Pieces and cutouts

lead.text: A shape made by joining or trimming simpler shapes is called a composite shape. The simplest kind is a rectangle with a corner taken out of it, and the piece taken out is the cutout.

The L-shaped floor works like that. Find the area of the whole rectangle as if the corner were still there, and subtract the area of the cutout, which is a smaller rectangle. What is left is the floor.

Take a floor shaped like an 8 m by 5 m rectangle with a 3 m by 2 m corner taken out. The whole rectangle has an area of 8 × 5 = 40 m² and the cutout has 3 × 2 = 6 m², so the floor is 40 − 6 = 34 m². You never need to measure the edges of the L itself.
Start from the whole rectangle.

There is a second way to reach the same answer. Instead of filling the corner in, cut the L into rectangles that fit together. A line drawn across the L splits it into two rectangles, and each has an area you can find directly. The floor's area is the two areas added.

This only works if the pieces fit properly. They must cover the whole floor with no gap, and they must not overlap. Where two pieces overlap, the overlapping region lies inside both, so adding their areas counts it twice and the total comes out too big. Check that every part of the shape sits in exactly one piece.

For example, a floor is a 7 m by 3 m rectangle with a 3 m by 4 m rectangle joined along a 3 m edge. The areas are 7 × 3 = 21 m² and 3 × 4 = 12 m², and together they give 33 m². Both methods always agree, so use whichever gives the easier numbers.
Two rectangles are joined edge to edge.
This L-shaped floor fits inside a 9 m by 7 m rectangle. The missing corner is 3 m by 2 m.

Not every shape is made of rectangles. A trapezoid has four sides, and exactly one pair of them is parallel. Those two parallel sides are its bases, and they have different lengths. The shape looks like a rectangle with one slanting end, and you meet it in road signs, bridge supports and the side of a bucket.

Its area looks hard to find, but a copy of the shape helps. Make a second trapezoid just like the first and turn it upside down. Slide it next to the first so that their slanting sides touch. The two make one parallelogram, and the parallelogram's base is the two bases laid end to end.
That parallelogram has the same height as each trapezoid, and the last lesson gave its area as base times height. What remains is to find what part of it one trapezoid is.
Think about how many copies it took to make the parallelogram.

Now put the pieces together. The parallelogram has a base of (top base + bottom base) and the same height, so its area is (top base + bottom base) × height. One trapezoid is half of that, so its area is ½ × (top base + bottom base) × height.

A trapezoid with bases of 9 cm and 5 cm and a height of 4 cm has an area of ½ × (9 + 5) × 4 = 28 cm². Averaging the two bases first gives the same result: (9 + 5) ÷ 2 = 7, and 7 × 4 = 28 cm². The average base is the width of a rectangle with the same area.
When the two bases are equal the shape is a parallelogram, and the formula gives base times height as before.
Use both parallel sides and the height between them.

blocks.text: A hall is 10 m long and 6 m wide, except that one corner of it is missing. A 4 m by 3 m piece has been walled off for a staircase, so the floor you can walk on is shaped like an L. A decorator wants to know how much of it needs varnish.

The difficulty is that an L is not a rectangle, so there is no single length times width to use. Most real shapes turn out to be made of simpler ones, though. A floor plan, a garden bed and a road sign can each be split into rectangles and triangles, or seen as one big rectangle with something missing.
This lesson looks at two ways of measuring the L and then uses the same thinking on a shape with slanting sides.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the area of an L shape two ways, and of a trapezoid by building a parallelogram.

recap.keyIdea: Add the areas of pieces that do not overlap, or subtract a cutout from the whole. A trapezoid is half a parallelogram.

blocks.text: Back at the hall, you found that the 10 m by 6 m floor with a 4 m by 3 m corner missing covers 48 m². You also added the two pieces of a patio to get 22 m².
