recap.nextHook: A circle has no straight sides to split into rectangles and no corners to cut away. The next lesson starts from the line between a circle's middle and its edge and works out what the edge and the inside need.

lessons.title: Around and inside circles

steps.headline: From the middle to the edge

lead.text: Take a dinner plate and put a finger on its exact middle. A straight line from that finger to the rim has the same length wherever you point it, and that sameness is what makes the plate round. The line is called the radius. On a plate with a radius of 10 cm, the whole rim sits 10 cm from the middle.

Now draw a line from one side of the rim to the other, passing through the middle. That line is the diameter. It is made of two radii laid end to end, one on each side of the middle, so for this plate the diameter is 2 × 10 = 20 cm.

afterFigure.text: Press Show diameter under the drawing to see the second half of the line. The two words answer different questions. The radius says how far the rim is from the middle, and the diameter says how wide the circle is.

A ruler measures across, so a size on a label is usually the diameter, while a formula may ask for the radius. Halving the diameter turns one into the other, and the first job with any circle is to find out which of the two you were given.

lead.text: The owner's card gives the middle-to-edge measurement. The box is chosen by the pizza's width.

Next comes the crust. The distance all the way round a circle is its circumference, and for the pizza it is the length of the strip the owner brushes with butter. Bending a tape measure round the edge would give it, but there is a rule that saves the effort.

Wrap a piece of string once round a round tin, then straighten it and measure it against a ruler. Measure the width of the tin across the middle as well. The string is always a little more than three times the width. A mug gives the same answer and so does a bicycle wheel. For a tin 8 cm across, the string comes to about 25 cm, which is 8 × 3.14.

That ratio is the same for every circle, and it has its own symbol, π (pronounced “pie”). Its digits never end, starting 3.14159, and 3.14 is close enough for everyday work, so this course uses 3.14. The distance round a circle is π times its diameter.
Roll a coin once along a table and it covers exactly the distance round its edge.

steps.headline: When you are given the radius

lead.text: The rule wants the diameter, and the owner's card gave the radius. The fix is to double the radius first. A bicycle wheel with a radius of 30 cm has a diameter of 60 cm, so its rim is 3.14 × 60 = 188.4 cm long.

Doubling and multiplying by π can be done in one step, because the diameter is 2 × the radius. The distance round is 2 × π × radius, and many books write it that way. For the wheel it gives 2 × 3.14 × 30 = 188.4 cm. Use the version that suits the number you are given.
A round badge is described by its radius, not its width. Decide what to do to the radius before you bring in π.
Now the cheese. It covers the whole top of the pizza, and the amount of surface covered is the area. Area is counted in squares, so the question becomes how many squares fit inside a circle.

Draw a square on the radius, with each side as long as the radius. On a pizza with a radius of 15 cm that square is 15 cm by 15 cm, and its area is 15 × 15 = 225 cm². The pizza holds a little over three of those squares. It holds exactly π of them, so its area is 3.14 × 225 = 706.5 cm².

That gives the rule. The area of a circle is π × radius × radius, because the radius takes part twice, once for each side of the square. Area is measured in square units, here cm², since squares were what we counted. The rule needs the radius itself, never the diameter.
Picture a square drawn on the disc's radius, and count how many of those squares the disc holds.

Most slips with circles come from using the wrong measurement, and the area rule is where they cost the most. A label on a round mat or a pizza box says how wide it is, so the number you read is the diameter. If that number goes straight into π × radius × radius, the radius used is twice as big as it should be, and the squaring makes the area four times too big.
So the first move is to ask what the number measures. If it is the distance across, halve it. A pizza box 40 cm across holds a pizza with a radius of 20 cm and an area of 3.14 × 20 × 20 = 1256 cm².
The mat's size is given across it. Decide whether that is the radius or the diameter before you start.

The shop also sells a larger pizza, so the owner wants to know what happens to the crust and the cheese when the radius changes. Look at where the radius appears in each rule. The distance round is 2 × π × radius, which has the radius once. The area is π × radius × radius, which has it twice.

That decides how each one grows. Make the radius ten times bigger and the distance round becomes ten times bigger, because the radius appears once. The area becomes 10 × 10 = 100 times bigger, because the radius appears twice and each appearance brings its own factor of ten. Larger pizzas gain cheese much faster than they gain crust.
The shop plans a pizza with twice the radius of its usual one. Count how many times the radius appears in each rule.

lessons.orientation: Use radius and diameter correctly in circumference and circle-area calculations.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Behind the counter of a small pizza shop the owner keeps one measurement on a card: 15 cm, from the middle of the pizza to its edge. Everything else has to be worked out from it. The box must be wide enough for the pizza to slide in. The crust gets brushed with garlic butter, so she wants to know how long it is. The cheese covers the whole top, so she also needs to know how much surface there is to cover.

None of this is hard with a ruler and one pizza. It gets awkward when the shop plans its sizes before making anything. A circle has no straight sides to count and no corners, so the rules for rectangles and triangles don't apply. What does help is that a circle is fixed by that single measurement from the middle to the edge.
The lesson takes the pizza through the shop in the order the owner needs the answers, starting with the width of the box. A bigger pizza comes at the end.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the distance round a circle and the space inside it, from either its radius or its diameter.

recap.keyIdea: The distance round a circle is π × diameter, and the area inside it is π × radius × radius. Check whether you are given the radius or the diameter.

blocks.text: The pizza measuring 15 cm from its middle to its edge is 30 cm across, so the box has to be at least that wide.
A circle with a radius of 3 cm has 18.84 cm round its edge and covers 28.26 cm². A mat 8 m across covers 50.24 m².

recap.nextHook: The shop's larger pizza has to look like the small one, only bigger. The next lesson starts with a photo being enlarged and works out how tall the print must be so that nothing looks stretched.

lessons.title: Same shape, new size

steps.headline: A copy that keeps its shape

lead.text: Try the squashing on paper. Draw a rectangle 2 cm wide and 3 cm tall, then draw another that is 4 cm wide and still 3 cm tall. The second one looks stretched, because its proportions have changed. A copy only looks like the original if the width and the height grow together.

The way to make that happen is to multiply every length by the same number. If the number is 4, the 2 cm width becomes 8 cm and the 3 cm height becomes 12 cm. The new rectangle has the same angles and the same proportions as the old one, so it looks like a bigger version. Two shapes related like this are called similar, and the number that every length is multiplied by is the scale factor.

afterFigure.text: You can also find a scale factor from one length before and after. Divide the new length by the old one. A 6 cm edge that becomes 9 cm has been multiplied by 9 ÷ 6 = 1.5, so every other length in the picture is multiplied by 1.5 as well.

lead.text: Back in the print shop, the snapshot is 4 cm wide and 3 cm tall, and the customer wants the enlargement to be 8 cm wide.

There is a tempting shortcut. In the snapshot the width grew by 4 cm, so it might seem fair to add 4 cm to the height as well. Adding the same amount to every side is the most common way for a copy to go wrong, because the sides grow by equal amounts while the shape changes.

Take a rectangle 1 cm wide and 2 cm tall and add 1 cm to each side. It becomes 2 cm by 3 cm. The tall side used to be twice the short side, and now it is only one and a half times as long, so the rectangle has a different shape. Multiplying both sides by 2 would give 2 cm by 4 cm, where the tall side is still twice the short one.
The same reasoning rules out changing only one length, as the squashed faces showed. A similar copy needs every length multiplied by one number, and nothing else keeps the shape.
A designer wants a bigger copy of a rectangle that keeps its shape exactly. She is choosing what to do to its sides.
A rectangle is 2 units wide and 3 units tall, and it is enlarged by scale factor 3.

So far the scale factor has been given. Often it is hidden in the problem and has to be found, as it was in the print shop. To find it, look for a length you know in both shapes. Lengths that sit in the same place on the two shapes, such as the width of the old photo and the width of the new one, are called corresponding. Dividing a new length by its corresponding old length gives the scale factor.

Take a triangle with sides 5 cm, 12 cm and 13 cm, and a larger similar triangle whose shortest side is 15 cm. The shortest sides correspond, and 15 ÷ 5 = 3. The scale factor is 3, so every other side is three times as long as its partner: 12 × 3 = 36 cm and 13 × 3 = 39 cm. One pair of matching sides is all it takes.
This time the factor isn't given. Match a side of the new triangle with its corresponding side in the old one.

A scale factor doesn't have to make things bigger. A factor of 1 gives an exact copy, and a factor between 0 and 1 gives a smaller one. A factor of 0.5 halves every length and 0.25 makes every length a quarter as long. The wallet-size snapshot could have been made from a poster in just this way.

A scale drawing works on the same idea. An architect draws a house on paper with every length shrunk by one factor, and the scale tells you how much. A scale of “1 cm represents 50 cm” means that every centimetre on the paper stands for 50 cm of house. A door drawn 4 cm tall is 4 × 50 = 200 cm tall in real life, which is 2 m, since 100 cm make 1 m.
The drawing and the house are similar shapes, and the scale is their scale factor.
A photograph is printed small enough for a wallet. Each length shrinks by the same factor.

lessons.orientation: Match corresponding lengths and apply one scale factor to every dimension.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A photographer has a snapshot that is 4 cm wide and 3 cm tall, small enough for a wallet. A friend would like it much bigger, and the print shop can make it as large as the customer likes. All the shop needs to know is the new size, and the customer says the photo should be 8 cm wide.

It sounds simple until you picture getting it wrong. If the shop makes the picture wider and leaves the height alone, everyone in the photo looks squashed flat. If it adds the same amount to each side, the faces come out a slightly different shape from the ones in the original. A good enlargement keeps everything looking as it did, only bigger.

That is the problem for this lesson: working out what has to happen to the height when the width has been decided. The same idea sits behind maps, architects' plans and model kits, wherever a small drawing or object stands in for a large one.

intro.promise: By the end you'll scale a shape up or down with one factor and find the factor from matching sides.

recap.keyIdea: Similar shapes have the same angles, and every length is multiplied by the same scale factor. Divide a new length by its matching old length to find it.

blocks.text: The snapshot that is 4 cm by 3 cm and is enlarged to 8 cm wide has to be 6 cm tall, because the width doubled and so the height must double.
A triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 and a shortest side of 9 has a longest side of 15 cm, and a width of 5 reduced by 0.5 comes to 2.5.

recap.nextHook: A print that is twice as wide and twice as tall uses more than twice as much paper. The next lesson counts how much more, starting from a small tile and a bigger copy of it.

lessons.title: When area scales

lead.text: To see how area changes, cover the big copy with copies of the small tile. Take a square tile and a larger copy whose sides are three times as long. Along one side of the big tile you can lay three small tiles. The big tile is also three small tiles tall, so there are three rows of them.

Counting gives 3 × 3 = 9 small tiles. The big tile has nine times the area of the small one, although its sides are only three times as long. The extra comes from the rows. A longer tile is also taller, and both changes add area.

afterFigure.text: The count follows the scale factor in both directions. With sides four times as long, four small tiles fit along an edge and there are four rows, so the big tile holds 4 × 4 = 16 small ones.

lead.text: Back at the tile shop. The small tile is 2 cm by 2 cm, and the large tile is a copy with sides twice as long.

Counting tiles works for squares, and other shapes need a rule. A rectangle's area is its width times its height. In a similar copy both of those lengths are multiplied by the scale factor, which we can call k. The new width is k times the old width, and the new height is k times the old height.

afterFigure.text: So the new area is (k × width) × (k × height), which equals k × k × (width × height). The old area has been multiplied by k × k, and that number is called the area factor. A rectangle 4 cm by 5 cm has an area of 20 cm². Scaling every length by 4 gives 16 cm by 20 cm. Its area is 320 cm², and 20 × 16 = 320 as the rule says.
The rule holds for any shape, as long as every length is multiplied by the same k. It breaks when only one length changes, because the second k is then missing.

lead.text: A square's area is its side times its side.

Often a problem gives an area and asks for the area of an enlargement, without any need for the sides. A logo might have an awkward outline that is hard to measure, but once its area is known the rule still works. Suppose a shape has area 8 cm² and a copy has every length tripled. The area factor is 3 × 3 = 9, so the copy has an area of 8 × 9 = 72 cm².

The rule also runs downwards. When the scale factor is less than 1, the copy is smaller and its area shrinks by the factor times itself. Halving every length gives an area factor of ½ × ½ = ¼. A shape of area 16 cm² has a half-size copy with area 4 cm², a quarter of the original.
Work out the area factor before you touch the area.

steps.headline: Going back to the length factor

lead.text: Sometimes the area factor is known and the length factor is the unknown. A map maker says that her new map has 49 times the area of the old one, and wants to know how much longer its lengths are. The area factor is the length factor times itself, so she needs the number that multiplies by itself to give 49.

That number is called the square root. The square root of 49 is 7, because 7 × 7 = 49, and so every length on the new map is 7 times as long. You can find a square root with the √ key on a calculator or by trying a few numbers. Squaring the answer gives you back the area factor, which is a check on your work.
A similar copy is described by its area, and the lengths are the unknown.
A designer stretches a banner in one direction only. Check which lengths actually change.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish a length scale factor from the resulting area factor.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A tile maker sells a small square tile, 2 cm on each side, and a larger tile that is an exact copy of it with every side twice as long. Both come in boxes that are priced by how much wall they cover.

The last lesson showed what happens to lengths in a copy: every one is multiplied by the scale factor. Covering a wall is not about lengths, though. It is about area, the amount of surface a tile covers, and a tile's area is made from two lengths, one across and one up. That raises a puzzle about what a scale factor does when it reaches both of them.

Printers, architects and people ordering paint all depend on the answer, because they need to know how much more paper, floor or paint a bigger copy takes. The lesson starts from the two tiles and builds the rule one step at a time.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find how area changes when every length is scaled, and go back from an area factor to a length factor.

recap.keyIdea: If every length is multiplied by k, the area is multiplied by k × k. Going back from an area factor to a length factor takes a square root.

blocks.text: A tile with sides twice as long holds 4 of the small tiles, and a shape of 6 cm² whose lengths are tripled covers 54 cm².
An area 9 times as big means the lengths are 3 times as long, and a banner stretched in one direction only has its area multiplied by 2.

recap.nextHook: Squares turn up in one more place. A walk of 3 m east and 4 m north has a shortcut across, and the next lesson shows how the squares of the two straight parts give the length of the shortcut.

lessons.title: Right-triangle distances

lead.text: Look at the garden from above. The path east and the path north meet at a right angle, a corner of 90°. The shortcut joins their far ends, and the three paths make a right triangle. The two sides that meet at the right angle are its legs. The side facing the right angle is the hypotenuse, which is always the longest.

afterFigure.text: Walking along the legs takes you further than walking along the hypotenuse. A straight line is the shortest distance between two points, and the bent route through the corner is always longer. How much longer depends on the lengths of the legs, and the next screens work out the exact amount.

lead.text: The garden path is 3 m east and then 4 m north. A friend suggests cutting across the lawn instead.

The shortcut turns out to follow a tidy rule. Draw a square on each side of the garden triangle, using the side as one edge of the square. The square on the 3 m leg has an area of 3 × 3 = 9 m², and the square on the 4 m leg has an area of 4 × 4 = 16 m². Add them and you get 25 m², which is the area of the square on the hypotenuse. A square with area 25 m² has sides 5 m long, so the shortcut is 5 m.

afterFigure.text: This holds for every right triangle, and it is called Pythagoras' theorem. If the legs are a and b and the hypotenuse is c, it says a² + b² = c². The small 2 means “times itself”. That gives c², and the square root from the last lesson turns it into c.
To find a hypotenuse, square each leg and add the squares. Then take the square root of the sum.

lead.text: A different triangle: the two legs are 5 m and 12 m.

Decide which side is which before using the rule on a new triangle. The hypotenuse faces the right angle, whichever way the triangle is turned. Standing on a corner or leaning to one side makes no difference. The hypotenuse always goes in the c position, and a leg put there by mistake gives a wrong answer.

There is also a check to run at the end. The hypotenuse is the longest side, so your answer must be longer than either leg. It must be shorter than the two legs added together, because that sum is the bent route round the corner. If the answer fails either test, look for a slip, such as forgetting the square root at the end.
Say which sides are the legs before you square anything, and check your answer against the two tests.

Sometimes the long side is known and a leg is missing. A tent has a rope that runs from the top of a pole down to a peg in the ground. The rope is the hypotenuse, the pole is one leg and the ground between the foot of the pole and the peg is the other. The rope and the ground distance are easy to measure, and the height of the pole is the one to work out.

The rule a² + b² = c² still holds, but now c² and one of the squares are known. Subtract the known square from c² to leave the missing one. A rope 13 m long with its peg 5 m from the pole gives 13² − 5² = 169 − 25 = 144, and the square root of 144 is 12, so the pole is 12 m tall.

The sign matters. Adding the squares finds the longest side. Subtracting the known leg's square from the hypotenuse's finds the other leg. If a leg comes out longer than the hypotenuse, the squares were added by mistake.
A brace holds up a shelf. Decide which side is the hypotenuse before you subtract.

lessons.orientation: Find a missing side using squared lengths and identify when the Pythagorean theorem applies.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You are crossing a garden. A path runs 3 m east along one edge of the lawn and then 4 m north along another, so the walk to the far corner is 7 m. A friend who is already standing there looks at the lawn and says that anyone who didn't mind the grass could have walked straight across.

She is right that a straight line is the shortest way between two points. The interesting question is how long it is. You can't always walk it first to find out. A builder checking whether a roof frame is square, or a window cleaner choosing a ladder, needs the length of a diagonal while knowing only the two straight parts that meet at a corner.
Those two parts meet at a right angle, and shapes with a right angle follow a rule that connects their sides. Squares, which the last lesson used to compare areas, play the main part in it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the longest side of a right triangle from the other two, and a missing short side from the longest.

recap.keyIdea: In a right triangle a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse. Add the squares of the legs to find c, or subtract the known leg's square from c² to find the other leg.

blocks.text: The garden path of 3 m east and 4 m north is 7 m long, and the straight way across is shorter, at 5 m.
Legs of 5 m and 12 m give a hypotenuse of 13 m, and a hypotenuse of 25 cm with one leg of 7 cm leaves a missing leg of 24 cm.

recap.nextHook: The garden is only one place where the rule works. On a map or a screen every point has a pair of numbers, and the distance between two points is the hypotenuse of a right triangle you can read off the grid. The next lesson starts with a drone flying between two such points.

lessons.title: Distance on a grid

steps.headline: How far apart on the grid

lead.text: A point on a grid is described by two numbers in brackets. The first says how far across the point is, and the second says how far up. So (2, 1) is two steps across and one step up from the place where the counting starts.

To find how far apart two points are in one direction, subtract. Take (2, 1) and (8, 4). The across numbers are 2 and 8, so the points are 8 − 2 = 6 units apart sideways. The up numbers are 1 and 4, so they are 4 − 1 = 3 units apart vertically. Each of these is a coordinate difference.

afterFigure.text: A negative coordinate puts a point on the other side of zero, so the gap has to be counted across zero. From −2 to 3 is 2 steps to reach zero and 3 more, which makes 5 units. Subtraction gives the same: 3 − (−2) = 5.

lead.text: Back to the drone, flying along the grid lines from A to B.

steps.headline: The straight flight is a hypotenuse

lead.text: The drone doesn't have to follow the streets. The route along the grid and the straight line from A to B make a right triangle. One leg is the sideways gap and the other is the vertical gap, and the two meet at a right angle because one runs across and the other runs straight up. The straight flight is the hypotenuse.
That puts the last lesson's rule to work. Take the points (1, 1) and (9, 16). The gaps are 9 − 1 = 8 and 16 − 1 = 15, so the distance is √(8² + 15²) = √(64 + 225) = √289 = 17 units.
A distance on a grid starts with subtraction, which gives the two gaps. The rest is the rule you already have. Square each gap and add the squares. Then take the square root of the sum.
The drone could fly straight from A (1, 2) to B (4, 6) instead of following the grid.

steps.headline: Points on either side of zero

lead.text: Negative coordinates cause most of the slips with distances, so it is worth working one through. Take the points (−5, −4) and (4, 8). The sideways gap runs across zero: 5 units to reach it and 4 more, which is 4 − (−5) = 9. The vertical gap does the same, since 8 − (−4) = 12.

The legs are 9 and 12. Squaring gives 81 and 144, and these add to 225. The square root of 225 is 15, so the points are 15 units apart. Dropping the minus sign from −5 would make the gap 4 − 5 = −1, and the distance would come out badly wrong.

A quick check helps here. When two coordinates lie on opposite sides of zero, the gap between them is their sizes added together, so it is larger than both. A smaller gap usually means a minus sign has been dropped.
Find how far apart the points are in each direction first, then use the right triangle they make.

Two more facts help with checking. The first is about moving a segment. Suppose the points (1, 1) and (4, 5) are both moved 5 units right and 3 units up, to (6, 4) and (9, 8). Each across number grew by 5, so their difference is still 9 − 6 = 3. Each up number grew by 3, so their difference is still 8 − 4 = 4. The gaps are 3 and 4 before and after, and so the distance is unchanged.

The second fact is about order. If you call the points the other way round, each subtraction comes out with the opposite sign. A square is never negative, so squaring the gaps wipes out the sign and the distance comes out the same. It doesn't matter which point you start from.
Both ends of a segment are moved: 2 units right and 1 unit up. Ask what happens to the gaps between them.

lessons.orientation: Use coordinate differences as right-triangle legs and distinguish direct distance from a grid path.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A delivery drone works in a town laid out like graph paper. Its base is marked A and the customer's house is marked B. Every place on the grid has two numbers, called its coordinates, which say how far across the point is and how far up. A is at (1, 2) and B is at (4, 6). On its usual route the drone keeps to the grid lines, flying east first and then north.

The drone's controller has no map to look at. It has two numbers for each place and has to work everything else out from them. It needs the distance along the grid lines, and it also needs the straight-line distance between A and B, which is the shortest flight it could make.

The last lesson gave a rule for the long side of a right triangle. This lesson shows that the rule works on a grid, where any two points are the corners of a right triangle that you can read straight from their coordinates.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find how far apart two points are in a straight line, from their coordinates.

recap.keyIdea: Subtract coordinates to get the horizontal and vertical gaps, then use them as the legs of a right triangle.

blocks.text: The drone's route along the grid from A to B is 7 units, and the straight flight is 5.
You also found 17 units from (1, 1) to (9, 16), 25 from (0, 1) to (7, 25), and found that sliding both ends of a segment leaves its length alone.

recap.nextHook: Flat shapes have areas, and the next lesson moves on to boxes. It starts with sugar cubes stacked in layers and asks how many of them fill the box.

lessons.title: Filling space

lead.text: Start with the layer you can see when the lid comes off. The cubes sit in rows, and every row holds the same number. If a row has 6 cubes and the layer has 3 rows, the layer holds 3 × 6 = 18 cubes, which is quicker to find than counting each one.

Under that layer sits another exactly like it, and under that another. If the box is two layers deep, it holds twice as many cubes as one layer, so 2 × 18 = 36. A box four layers deep would hold 4 × 18 = 72. Each new layer adds the same number again, which is why multiplying works.

afterFigure.text: Switch between the two boxes. The layer is the same size in both, and only the number of layers changes. To find the cubes in a box, multiply the cubes in a row by the number of rows, then multiply by the number of layers. A cube that is exactly 1 cm along every edge is called a unit cube, and the boxes in this lesson are all measured in them.

lead.text: Use the layers-and-rows method on a real box. Find how many cubes make one layer first.

The number of unit cubes that fill a space is called its volume, so the box with two layers of 18 cubes has a volume of 36 unit cubes. If each unit cube is 1 cm along every edge, the volume is given in cubic centimetres. Here that is 36 cubic centimetres, written 36 cm³.

The unit follows from how many directions you measure in. A length goes in one direction and is measured in centimetres. An area covers a flat surface with squares 1 cm by 1 cm, so it is measured in square centimetres, cm². Volume fills space with cubes 1 cm by 1 cm by 1 cm, and each cube reaches along, across and up. That third direction is why the small raised 3 appears.
Bigger spaces use bigger units in the same way. A room might have a volume of 40 cubic metres, written 40 m³, which is 40 cubes with edges 1 m long.
Think about how many directions you need to measure in to fill a box.

You don't have to build a box out of cubes to count them, because its three measurements tell you everything. Take a box 9 cm long, 2 cm wide and 3 cm high. Rows of 9 cubes run along its length, and 2 of those rows fit across its width, so the bottom layer holds 9 × 2 = 18 cubes. That number is also the area of the base in square centimetres, because each cube stands on a 1 cm by 1 cm square of the floor.

The height says how many layers there are. A height of 3 cm means 3 layers, so the box holds 18 × 3 = 54 cubes, a volume of 54 cm³. As a rule, volume = base area × height, and since the base area is length × width, that is length × width × height.

afterFigure.text: The second drawing is the same box stood on its end. Its base is 3 by 2, which holds 6 cubes, and there are 9 layers, so 6 × 9 = 54 again. Any face can be the base, because multiplying three numbers gives the same answer in whatever order you take them.

lead.text: This box is 4 cm long, 3 cm wide and 2 cm high. Picture one layer of unit cubes, then the layers stacked on it.

reveal.text: You counted one layer of 4 × 3 and stacked two of them. Length × width × height counts every cube once.

steps.headline: A box is 6 cm long, 2 cm wide and 4 cm high. Find its volume.

workedSteps.text: Find the cubes in one layer.

steps.headline: A box is 4 cm long, 3 cm wide and 5 cm high. Find its volume.

workedSteps.text: Find the cubes in one layer.

lead.text: So far you have been given the box and asked for its volume. Sometimes it goes the other way: you know how much a box holds and one measurement is missing. The multiplication can be run backwards. Take a box that holds 96 cm³ with a base 8 cm by 3 cm, and suppose its height is the missing piece.
Each layer holds 8 × 3 = 24 cubes, so the question is how many layers of 24 cubes make 96. Fitting equal groups into a total is division: 96 ÷ 24 = 4. The box has 4 layers, so it is 4 cm high.

afterFigure.text: Check by multiplying forwards: 24 × 4 = 96, the volume you started with. Divide the volume by the base area to get the height, and multiply the base area by the height to get the volume back. Each step undoes the other.

lead.text: The box has a volume, a length and a width. Work out how many cubes fit in one layer, then how many layers make the total.

A cube is a box whose length, width and height are all equal, so one number, its side, describes it. Take a cube with sides 3 cm. Its bottom layer is 3 × 3 = 9 cubes and there are 3 layers, so its volume is 9 × 3 = 27 cm³. In short that is side × side × side, written 3³ and read as three cubed.

Cubes of different sizes show how quickly the volume grows. A cube with side 1 cm holds 1 cm³, and one with side 2 cm holds 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cm³. Doubling the side makes room for eight times as many unit cubes, because the layer grows in two directions and the number of layers grows as well.

afterFigure.text: For a cube with side s, the volume is s × s × s, whatever the size.

lead.text: A cube has three equal edges. Use its side in all three places.

lessons.orientation: Count volume in cubic units, then work back from a volume to a missing height.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A café keeps its sugar in flat cardboard boxes packed with sugar cubes, and every cube is exactly 1 cm along each edge. Lift the lid and you can see the top layer: neat rows of white squares with no gaps between them. Underneath there are more layers packed the same way, but you can't see them.

The person who orders the supplies wants to know how many sugar cubes a box holds. Taking them all out to count would take ages and would spoil the packing, so a better way is needed, one that uses only the box itself. Its length, its width and its height are all you can measure from outside.

In the last lesson every shape was flat, and one number, its area, said how much surface it covered. A box has depth as well as length and width, so it needs a new kind of measurement. This lesson shows how to count what fits inside a box from those three measurements.

intro.promise: By the end you'll work out what a box holds from its three measurements, and its height from what it holds.

recap.keyIdea: Volume is length × width × height, in cubic units. Divide by the base area to find a missing height.

blocks.text: You counted 30 cubes in 3 layers of 10, and learned that the count is called volume, measured in cubic units.
You also found 60 cm³ for a box 4 by 3 by 5 and 216 cm³ for a cube with sides of 6 cm. Working back from 120 cm³ gave a height of 5 cm.

recap.nextHook: A box has an outside as well as an inside. A present in a box needs wrapping paper over every face, and the next lesson unfolds a box flat to measure how much.

lessons.title: Unfolding surface area

steps.headline: Unfolding a box into a net

lead.text: Take an empty cereal box and cut along some of its edges until it lies flat on the table. The flat shape you get is called a net. It is made of rectangles joined along the edges you didn't cut, and every flat side of the box, called a face, appears in it exactly once.

Because the net is flat, it can be measured with areas you already know how to find. The total area of all the faces is the surface area of the box. It is also the area of paper that wraps the box exactly, with no overlaps.

afterFigure.text: Look at which faces match. The top and the bottom are the same size. So are the front and the back, and so are the two ends. The faces of a box come in pairs, and that pattern shortens the work.

lead.text: Use the pairs of matching faces from the net.

The easiest box to wrap is a cube. Its edges are all the same length, so all six faces are identical squares. For a cube with sides 2 cm long, each face is a square 2 cm by 2 cm, with an area of 2 × 2 = 4 cm². The paper has to cover six of those faces, so the surface area is 6 × 4 = 24 cm². In words, find the area of one face and multiply by 6.

afterFigure.text: The unit differs from the last lesson, where cubes measured the space inside a box in cubic centimetres. Paper covers only the outside, which is a flat surface, so its area is measured in square centimetres, cm².

lead.text: Use the cube method: the area of one face, then all of the faces.

A box that is longer than it is wide has faces of different sizes, and the matching pairs still help. Take a pencil case 10 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm high. The top and the bottom are each 10 × 4 = 40 cm². The front and the back are each 10 × 3 = 30 cm². The two ends are each 4 × 3 = 12 cm².

Only three different faces appear, and each one appears twice. Add the three areas to get 40 + 30 + 12 = 82 cm². Then double that total to cover the matching faces: 2 × 82 = 164 cm². The surface area of the pencil case is 164 cm².

afterFigure.text: As a rule, surface area = 2 × (length × width + length × height + width × height). Doubling once at the end is quicker than adding six areas, and it makes it harder to forget a face.

steps.headline: A closed box is 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm. Find its surface area.

workedSteps.text: Add them, then double for the matching faces.

steps.headline: A closed box is 5 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm. Find its surface area.

lead.text: Plenty of boxes have no lid, such as a shoebox with its lid off, a fish tank or a bin. The paper or glass only has to cover the faces that are there. So find the surface area of the closed box first, then take away the area of the face that is missing.
Take the 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm box from the worked example, whose closed surface area is 52 cm². If its top is missing, that top was 4 × 3 = 12 cm², so the open box has 52 − 12 = 40 cm².

afterFigure.text: Check by adding the five faces that remain. The base is 12 cm². The two long sides are 4 × 2 = 8 cm² each and the two ends are 3 × 2 = 6 cm² each, which makes 28 cm² between them. Then 12 + 28 = 40 cm², the same answer. Only the missing face comes off. Its partner on the opposite side is still there and still counts.

lead.text: Find the area of the closed box first, then take away the lid.

reveal.text: Closed total, minus the missing face. Only the face that is missing comes off.

lead.text: Suppose the same present comes in two sizes of one shape, and every length of the bigger box is double the smaller one's. Take a small box 2 cm long, 1 cm wide and 1 cm high. Its three different faces are 2, 2 and 1 cm², so its surface area is 2 × (2 + 2 + 1) = 10 cm². Its volume is 2 × 1 × 1 = 2 cm³.

Double every length to get a box 4 cm long, 2 cm wide and 2 cm high. Its faces are now 8, 8 and 4 cm², so the surface area is 2 × (8 + 8 + 4) = 40 cm², which is four times as much. The volume is 4 × 2 × 2 = 16 cm³, which is eight times as much.

afterFigure.text: The reason is how many lengths are multiplied. An area multiplies two lengths, and doubling both makes it 2 × 2 = 4 times as big, as with the tiles earlier in the course. A volume multiplies three lengths, so doubling all three gives 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. In general, area goes up by the scale factor squared and volume by the scale factor cubed.

lead.text: Think about how many lengths are multiplied together in an area, and in a volume.

lessons.orientation: Unfold a box to find the paper it needs, and see how that amount grows with the box.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A present in a box sits on the table, and the wrapping paper is on a roll beside it. The paper has to cover the whole outside of the box at once: the top, the bottom and all four sides, with no gaps. Cut too little and a patch of box shows through. Cut too much and the spare paper is folded away and wasted.

The last lesson counted what fits inside a box. Wrapping needs a different measurement, because paper touches the outside and doesn't care what is in the box. Paper is flat, so the answer is a flat area, in the same kind of unit as a floor or a field.

Every shape so far was flat to begin with. A box isn't, but there is a way to flatten it. Cut along some of its edges and fold it open, and the outside spreads out on the table where you can measure it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find how much paper wraps a box, and how that amount changes when every length doubles.

recap.keyIdea: Surface area is the total area of all faces: twice the sum of three different faces, less any face that is missing.

blocks.text: You found that a cube-shaped gift box with sides 3 cm long needs 54 cm² of paper.
You also found 62 cm² for a box 5 by 3 by 2, 47 cm² when its lid is missing, 96 cm² for a cube with sides of 4 cm, and 248 cm² when a box of 62 cm² has every length doubled.

recap.nextHook: Boxes are not the only things that get wrapped. A tin has a curved side as well as flat ends. Cut along the curved side and unroll it, and the same idea of a net still applies.

questions.prompt: A 90° corner contains a 35° angle. How many degrees remain?
hints: Identify the total turn of the corner.
Subtract the known part from the total.
Calculate 90 − 35.
questions.onCorrect: The two parts fill the corner, so they add to 90°. Take the part you know from the whole.

misconceptions.feedback: 35° is the part you were given. The question asks for the part that is left.
That adds the 35° to the corner. The two parts together make the corner, not more.

questions.prompt: Two angles sit side by side on a straight line. One is 68°. What is the other, in degrees?
hints: A straight line represents a half-turn.
The adjacent angles add to 180°.
Calculate 180 − 68.
questions.onCorrect: The other angle is 180° − 68° = 112°: the two angles fill the half-turn.

misconceptions.feedback: 68° is the angle you were given. Find the part that is left.
That adds 180 to 68. The whole is 180°, so the other part is smaller than that.

questions.prompt: A pointer has turned 140°. How many more degrees complete a full 360° turn in the same direction?
hints: Use a full turn as the total.
Find the turn that has not yet been made.
Calculate 360 − 140.
questions.onCorrect: 220°. The turn so far and the turn left make a full 360°.

misconceptions.feedback: 140° is the turn already made. Find the part still to come.
That is 180 − 140. A full turn is 360°, not 180°.

questions.prompt: The arms of an angle are drawn twice as long, along the same lines. What happens to its size in degrees?
hints: Separate the length of a ray from its direction.

acceptedIdeas: It stays the same
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The degree measure depends on the directions of the rays, so extending them leaves the angle unchanged.

questions.onCorrect: The angle stays the same. It measures how far you turn, not how long the arms are.

misconceptions.feedback: A longer arm covers more paper, not more turn. The directions of the arms haven't changed.
Nothing was cut. The arms point the same way, so the turn is the same.

questions.prompt: A right angle is split into 27° and another angle. Find the other angle in degrees.
hints: A right angle is the whole.
Subtract the part already given.
Calculate 90 − 27.
questions.onCorrect: 63°. The parts of a right angle add to 90°, so subtract the part you know.

misconceptions.feedback: 117° comes from starting at 180°. A right angle is a quarter-turn, so start from 90°.
27° is the part you were given. Find the other part.

questions.prompt: Which pair of angles can sit side by side to form a straight angle?
hints: Add each pair and compare with a half-turn.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 72° + 108° = 180°, the measure of a straight angle.

questions.onCorrect: 72° + 108° = 180°. Two angles on a straight line fill a half-turn.

misconceptions.feedback: Those add to 90°, a right angle. A straight angle is a half-turn.
Those add to more than a half-turn: 190°.

questions.prompt: A triangle has angles 48° and 67°. What is its third angle in degrees?
hints: All three angles of a triangle together make 180°.
Add the two angles you are given.
Subtract 48 + 67 from 180.
questions.onCorrect: 65°. Take the two angles you know from 180°.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the two angles added. The third angle is what is left of 180°.
That leaves out the 67° angle. All three angles share the total.

questions.prompt: A right triangle has another angle of 32°. Find its third angle in degrees.
hints: The right angle uses half of the triangle's total.
The two acute angles add to 90°.
Calculate 90 − 32.
questions.onCorrect: 58°. Take the right angle and the 32° from 180°. The two sharp angles share 90°.

misconceptions.feedback: 90° is the right angle you already have. Find the third angle.
That leaves out the right angle. Take it from 180° as well.

questions.prompt: A triangle has two equal angles and a third angle of 44°. Find one of the equal angles in degrees.
hints: Take the unequal angle from 180°.
Split what remains equally between two angles.
Halve the leftover.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The equal angles share 180 − 44 = 136°; each is 136/2 = 68°.

questions.onCorrect: 68°. The two equal angles share what the third leaves, so halve it.

misconceptions.feedback: 136° is what the two equal angles share. Each gets half of it.
44° is the third angle, which you were given. Find the equal pair.

questions.prompt: Can a triangle have two right angles?
hints: Add up what two right angles use.

acceptedIdeas: No, the third angle would have nothing left.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, the third angle would have nothing left.

choices.label: Yes, if its sides are long enough.
No, the third angle would have nothing left.
Yes, if its third angle is also 90°.

questions.onCorrect: No. Two right angles use all 180°, so there is nothing left for a third angle.

misconceptions.feedback: Side length doesn't change the total. The three angles of any triangle add to 180°.
Three right angles would add to 270°, far past 180°.

questions.prompt: A triangular sign has angles 39° and 86°. Find its third angle in degrees.
hints: Treat all three angles as parts of 180°.
Find the total of the two given angles.
Calculate 180 − (39 + 86).
questions.onCorrect: 55°. Whatever the shape, the other two angles leave 180° minus their sum.

misconceptions.feedback: That's 39 + 86. The third angle is what is left of 180°.
That leaves out the 86° angle. Take both known angles from 180°.

questions.prompt: Which set can be the interior angles of a triangle?
hints: Check both the total and whether every angle is positive.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 40° + 60° + 80° = 180° and all three measures are positive.

questions.onCorrect: 40° + 60° + 80° = 180°. A triangle's angles must add to exactly 180°.

misconceptions.feedback: Those add to 210°, which is too much.
Those add to 190°, which is too much.

questions.prompt: Rectangle A is 6 m by 4 m and rectangle B is 8 m by 2 m. Which statement is true?
hints: Add the sides round each rectangle.
Count the rows of squares in each, then the squares per row.
Compare the two boundary totals, then the two square counts.

acceptedIdeas: They have the same perimeter but different areas
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both perimeters are 20, while their areas are 24 and 16 square units.

choices.label: They have the same perimeter but different areas
They have the same area but different perimeters
They have equal areas and equal perimeters

questions.onCorrect: Equal perimeters can hide different areas. Add the sides for one, count squares for the other.

misconceptions.feedback: Add the four sides of each rectangle. Do the two totals really differ?
Count the squares in each rectangle. Do they hold the same number?

questions.prompt: Find the perimeter of a rectangle 6 units long and 4 units wide.
hints: Perimeter is the total boundary.
There are two sides of each length.
Calculate 2 × (6 + 4).
questions.onCorrect: Perimeter adds all four sides. Opposite sides are equal, so two of each length.

misconceptions.feedback: That's 6 × 4, the area. Perimeter is the distance round the edge.
That's 6 + 4, only half the boundary. Count all four sides.

questions.prompt: Find the area of a rectangle 6 units long and 4 units wide, in square units.
hints: Count square units inside the boundary.
Use the number of rows and squares in each row.
Multiply 6 by 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six squares per row across four rows give 6 × 4 = 24 square units.

questions.onCorrect: Area counts squares inside: 4 rows of 6, so 6 × 4, in square units.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the distance round the edge. Area counts the squares inside.
That adds 6 + 4. Area multiplies rows by squares in each row.

questions.prompt: A rectangle is 7 units by 3 units. What area does it cover in square units?
hints: Area counts the inside.
Multiply the two perpendicular dimensions.
Calculate 7 × 3.
questions.onCorrect: 21 square units. Rows times squares per row gives the area of any rectangle.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the distance round the edge. Area counts the squares inside.
That adds 7 + 3. Area multiplies the two sides.

questions.prompt: A rectangular floor has area 54 m² and width 6 m. Find its length in metres.
hints: Area is length times width.
Undo multiplication by the known width.
Divide 54 by 6.
questions.onCorrect: 9 m. Area is length × width, so divide the area by the width to undo it.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies 54 by 6. Division undoes multiplying.
That takes 6 away. The area is the length times 6, so undo the multiplying.

questions.prompt: Which unit is appropriate for the area of a small floor?
hints: A unit square has both length and width.

acceptedIdeas: Square metres
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Area counts two-dimensional coverage, so it uses square metres.

questions.onCorrect: Square metres. Area counts squares, so it is measured in squares of a length unit.

misconceptions.feedback: Metres measure a length. Area counts squares.
Cubic metres measure space with three directions. A floor's cover has two.

questions.prompt: A triangle has base 8 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm. Find its area in square centimetres.
hints: Picture the rectangle with the same base and height.
A triangle covers half that rectangle.
Work out 8 × 5, then halve it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Half the enclosing rectangle gives 8 × 5 / 2 = 20 cm².

questions.onCorrect: 20 cm². A triangle is half the rectangle with the same base and height: 8 × 5 ÷ 2.

misconceptions.feedback: 40 is the whole 8 by 5 rectangle. A triangle covers half of it.
That adds 8 + 5. Multiply the base by the height, then halve.

questions.prompt: A triangle has a base of 8 cm, and its top corner is 5 cm above the base. The top corner slides sideways but stays 5 cm above the base. What happens to the triangle's area?
hints: Identify which dimensions enter the area formula.

acceptedIdeas: It stays the same
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The base and perpendicular height remain fixed, so base × height / 2 remains unchanged.

choices.label: It increases with the sloping side

questions.onCorrect: The area stays the same. Sliding the top corner keeps the base and the height unchanged.

misconceptions.feedback: The sloping sides change length, but the area uses the height. Does the height change?
The triangle is still there, with the same base and the same height.

questions.prompt: A parallelogram has base 8 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm. Find its area in square centimetres.
hints: A diagonal cuts the parallelogram into two triangles.
Each triangle has area base × height ÷ 2. How many are there?
Two halves make a whole: base × height.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two equal-area triangles together cover 8 × 5 = 40 cm².

questions.onCorrect: 40 cm². A parallelogram is two equal triangles, so halving cancels: base × height.

misconceptions.feedback: That's one triangle. The parallelogram is made of two.
That adds the base and height. Area multiplies them.

questions.prompt: Find the area of a triangle with base 7 m and perpendicular height 6 m, in square metres.
hints: Use the base and the perpendicular height.
Take half their product.
Calculate 7 × 6 / 2.
questions.onCorrect: 21 m². Halve base × perpendicular height, wherever the top corner sits.

misconceptions.feedback: 42 is the whole 7 by 6 rectangle. A triangle is half of it.
That adds 7 + 6. Multiply, then halve.

questions.prompt: A triangle has area 42 cm² and base 12 cm. Find its perpendicular height in centimetres.
hints: Reverse the triangle area formula.
Double the area before dividing by the base.
Calculate 2 × 42 / 12.
questions.onCorrect: 7 cm. Double the area, then divide by the base.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides 42 by 12 only. Base × height is twice the area, so double first.
That multiplies 42 by 12. Undo the multiplying with division.

questions.prompt: Which distance is the height used with a chosen triangle base?
hints: Look for the right-angle relationship to the base.

acceptedIdeas: The perpendicular distance from the opposite vertex to the base line
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The height must meet the line containing the chosen base at a right angle.

choices.label: The perpendicular distance from the opposite vertex to the base line

questions.onCorrect: Height is the perpendicular distance from the opposite corner to the base's line.

misconceptions.feedback: A sloping side leans away from the base. The height meets the base at a right angle.
A perimeter is a distance round the edge, and has nothing to do with height.

questions.prompt: A 9 m by 7 m floor has a 3 m by 2 m corner removed. Find the remaining area in square metres.
hints: Find the area before removing the corner.
Find the corner's area separately.
Calculate 9 × 7 − 3 × 2.
questions.onCorrect: 57 m². Whole rectangle minus the corner: 63 − 6.

misconceptions.feedback: 63 m² is the whole 9 by 7 rectangle. The corner is not part of the floor.
6 m² is the missing corner. The floor is what is left.

questions.prompt: You split a shape into two rectangles. What must be true before you add their areas?
hints: Is any part missing, or counted twice?

acceptedIdeas: They must cover the floor exactly without overlapping
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A disjoint partition counts every part of the floor exactly once.

choices.label: They must overlap as much as possible
They must cover the floor exactly without overlapping

questions.onCorrect: The pieces must cover the shape exactly, with no overlap and no gaps, so every part is counted once.

misconceptions.feedback: Overlapping parts would be counted twice.
Perimeters don't matter when adding areas. Ask whether every part is counted exactly once.

questions.prompt: A trapezoid has parallel bases 10 cm and 6 cm, with perpendicular height 4 cm. Find its area in square centimetres.
hints: Use both parallel bases.
Average their lengths, then multiply by height.
Calculate (10 + 6) × 4 / 2.
questions.onCorrect: 32 cm². Average the bases, then multiply by the height.

misconceptions.feedback: 40 cm² is the 10 by 4 rectangle. The top base is shorter.
That is two trapezoids' worth, a parallelogram. One trapezoid is half.

questions.prompt: A 12 cm by 8 cm rectangle has a 5 cm by 3 cm corner removed. Find the remaining area in square centimetres.
hints: Treat the missing part as a separate rectangle.
Subtract its area from the full rectangle.
Calculate 12 × 8 − 5 × 3.
questions.onCorrect: 81 cm². Outer rectangle minus the cutout: 96 − 15.

misconceptions.feedback: 96 cm² is the whole 12 by 8 rectangle. The cutout is not part of the shape.
15 cm² is the removed corner. Find what is left.

questions.prompt: A trapezoid has parallel bases 13 m and 7 m and perpendicular height 5 m. Find its area in square metres.
hints: Area uses the average of the two parallel bases.
Multiply that average by perpendicular height.
Calculate (13 + 7) × 5 / 2.
questions.onCorrect: 50 m². Average the two parallel bases and multiply by the height.

misconceptions.feedback: That is two trapezoids fitted into a parallelogram. One trapezoid is half.
That is 13 × 5. The top base is shorter than 13.

questions.prompt: Two area pieces overlap in a 4 m² region. Adding their areas counts that region how many times?
hints: How many of the two pieces contain the overlap?

acceptedIdeas: Twice
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The overlap belongs to both pieces, so the sum counts it twice. Subtract one copy when finding their combined area.

questions.onCorrect: Twice. The overlap lies in both pieces, so adding counts it in each.

misconceptions.feedback: The overlap is inside both pieces, so it is counted at least once.
Each piece includes the overlap. How many pieces is that?

questions.prompt: A circle has radius 3 cm. Find its diameter in centimetres.
hints: The diameter crosses the entire circle through its centre.
It contains a radius on each side of the centre.
Multiply the radius by two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A diameter contains two radii: 2 × 3 = 6 cm.

questions.onCorrect: 6 cm. A diameter is two radii laid end to end.

misconceptions.feedback: 3 cm is the radius you were given. The diameter goes right across.
That halves the radius. The diameter is longer than the radius.

questions.prompt: A round badge has a radius of 3 cm. Use π ≈ 3.14 to find the distance round its edge, in centimetres.
hints: Circumference measures the rim.
Multiply the diameter by π.
Calculate 2 × 3.14 × 3.
questions.onCorrect: 18.84 cm. Circumference is π × diameter, or 2 × π × radius.

misconceptions.feedback: 6 cm is only the diameter. Multiply it by π.
That is the area, which uses r × r. Circumference is the distance round.

questions.prompt: A disc has radius 3 cm. Use π ≈ 3.14 to find its area in square centimetres.
hints: Area covers the disc.
Square the radius, then multiply by π.
Calculate 3.14 × (3 × 3).
questions.onCorrect: 28.26 cm². Area is π × radius × radius.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the distance round. Area is the space inside: π × r × r.
That is π × 3. The radius is used twice: r × r.
That squares the radius but leaves out π.

questions.prompt: A circular mat is 8 m across. Use π ≈ 3.14 to find its area in square metres.
hints: The given distance is the diameter.
Halve it to obtain the radius before squaring.
Calculate 3.14 × (8/2)².
questions.onCorrect: 50.24 m². The mat is 8 across, so the radius is 4 before you square it.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses 8 as the radius. The mat is 8 across, which is the diameter.
That is π × 8. Area needs the radius multiplied by itself, then π.

questions.prompt: A circle's radius doubles. What happens to its circumference and its area?
hints: Compare 2πr with πr².

acceptedIdeas: Circumference doubles and area quadruples
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Circumference contains one radius factor; area contains two, so their multipliers are 2 and 2².

questions.onCorrect: Circumference doubles and area quadruples. Circumference uses r once, area uses r twice.

misconceptions.feedback: Area uses the radius twice (r × r), so it grows by more than the radius does.
Circumference uses the radius once, so it grows only as fast as the radius.

questions.prompt: Which measurement determines the length of trim around a circular table?
hints: Identify whether you need the boundary or the covered surface.

acceptedIdeas: Its circumference
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Trim follows the one-dimensional boundary, so its length is the circumference.

questions.onCorrect: Its circumference. Trim runs along the edge, and the circumference is the distance round.

misconceptions.feedback: Area is the space inside. Trim runs along the edge.
Volume needs three dimensions. A table's edge is a length.

questions.prompt: A rectangle 2 units wide and 3 units tall is enlarged by scale factor 3. What is the new width?
hints: A scale factor multiplies a length.
Apply it to the corresponding width.
Calculate 2 × 3.
questions.onCorrect: 6. The scale factor multiplies the width: 2 × 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 3 to the width. A scale factor multiplies.

questions.prompt: The same rectangle's original height is 3 units. What is its new height?
hints: The height uses the same multiplier as the width.
Multiply the original height by the scale factor.
Calculate 3 × 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Every length uses the same factor: 3 × 3 = 9 units.

questions.onCorrect: 9. The height uses the same factor: 3 × 3.

misconceptions.feedback: 6 is the new width. The height needs the same factor applied to its own length.

questions.prompt: Which change guarantees a similar copy of a rectangle?
hints: Similarity uses a common ratio, not a common added amount.

acceptedIdeas: Double every side length
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Multiplying every length by the same positive factor preserves angles and proportions.

choices.label: Add 2 units to its width and height

questions.onCorrect: Doubling every side keeps the shape. Multiplying all lengths by one factor makes a similar copy.

misconceptions.feedback: Doubling only the width stretches the rectangle sideways, changing its shape.
Adding is not multiplying. Adding 2 to a 2 by 4 rectangle gives 4 by 6, a different shape.

questions.prompt: A 5-unit width is reduced by scale factor 0.5. What is the new width?
hints: A factor below one makes a smaller copy.
Multiplying by one-half halves the width.
Split the original width into two equal lengths.
questions.onCorrect: 2.5. A factor below 1 shrinks every length: 5 × 0.5.

misconceptions.feedback: That doubles the width. A factor below one makes a smaller copy.
That takes 0.5 away. A scale factor multiplies.

questions.prompt: On a scale drawing, 1 cm represents 200 cm. A wall is drawn 3 cm long. Find its real length in metres.
hints: First use the drawing-to-real scale factor.
Then convert centimetres to metres.
Calculate (3 × 200)/100.
questions.onCorrect: 6 m. 3 × 200 = 600 cm, which is 6 m.

misconceptions.feedback: That is in centimetres. The question asks for metres.
That divides by 100 twice. Convert 600 cm to metres once.

questions.prompt: Two rectangles have equal areas. What can you say about whether they are similar?
hints: Area gives a product, not the ratio of dimensions.

acceptedIdeas: Area alone does not determine whether they are similar
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Different width-to-height ratios can produce the same area. Similarity requires matching proportions.

choices.label: Area alone does not determine whether they are similar

questions.onCorrect: Equal areas do not make shapes similar. Similar shapes share angles and a ratio of lengths.

misconceptions.feedback: Rectangles 2 by 6 and 3 by 4 have equal areas but different shapes.
Rectangles 2 by 6 and 3 by 4 have equal areas and different widths.

questions.prompt: A 3 cm by 2 cm rectangle has both lengths doubled. Find the new area in square centimetres.
hints: Find the new width and the new height.
Multiply them to get the new area.
Work out 6 × 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The new rectangle is 6 by 4: 6 × 4 = 24 cm².

questions.onCorrect: 24 cm². Both lengths doubled, so the area is multiplied by 2 × 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That only doubles the area. Both the width and the height doubled.
That adds 4 to the area, but scaling multiplies lengths.

questions.prompt: A shape has area 6 cm². Every length is tripled in a similar copy. Find the new area in square centimetres.
hints: Area changes in two dimensions.
Square the length scale factor.
Calculate 6 × 3 × 3.
questions.onCorrect: 54 cm². Area factor 3 × 3 = 9, so 6 × 9.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by 3 only. The factor works in two directions.
9 is the area factor. Multiply the area 6 by it.

questions.prompt: A shape has area 14 m². Every length is multiplied by 4 in a similar copy. Find the new area in square metres.
hints: Use the area factor, not just the length factor.
Multiply the original area by the square of four.
Calculate 14 × 4 × 4.
questions.onCorrect: 224 m². Area factor 4 × 4 = 16, and 14 × 16.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by 4 once. Area has two lengths, so use the factor twice.
16 is the area factor. Multiply the original area by it.

questions.prompt: A banner's width doubles while its height stays the same. By what number is its area multiplied?
hints: Track which dimensions change.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only one factor in width × height doubles, so the area doubles.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Only the width changes, so the area is multiplied only once by 2.

misconceptions.feedback: Squaring only applies when both lengths change. Here the height stays fixed.
8 is 2 × 2 × 2. Area has two lengths, and only one of them doubled.

questions.prompt: Three angles meet at a point and fill the whole turn. Two of them are 100° and 150°. What is the third, in degrees?
hints: What is the total of all three angles round a point?
Add the two angles you know.
Take that sum from the total.
questions.onCorrect: 110°. Angles round a point fill a full turn, so they add to 360°.

misconceptions.feedback: 250° is the two angles added together. The third angle is what is left of the turn.
That is 180 − 100. Round a point the total is 360°, not 180°.

questions.prompt: A hall is 10 m long and 6 m wide, and a 4 m by 3 m corner of it is missing. What area does the floor cover, in square metres?
hints: Find the area of the full 10 m by 6 m rectangle first.
The missing corner is a smaller rectangle. What is its area?
Take the missing corner from the full rectangle.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The corner is 4 × 3 = 12. The floor is 10 × 6 − 12 = 48 m².

questions.onCorrect: 48 m². Measure the whole rectangle, then take away the part that is missing.

misconceptions.feedback: 60 m² is the full rectangle. The missing corner is not floor.
12 m² is the missing corner. The floor is what is left.

questions.prompt: A patio is a 6 m by 2 m rectangle with a 2 m by 5 m rectangle joined below it. They do not overlap. What is its area, in square metres?
hints: Find the area of each rectangle.
Do the pieces overlap?
Add the two areas.
questions.onCorrect: 22 m². The pieces do not overlap, so their areas simply add.

misconceptions.feedback: 12 m² is the top piece only. Add the lower piece too.
That adds the sides. Find each piece's area, then add the areas.

questions.prompt: A 15 m by 10 m field has a pond in one corner that measures 6 m by 5 m. What area is left for grass, in square metres?
hints: Find the area of the whole field.
Find the area of the pond.
Take the pond from the field.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The pond is 6 × 5 = 30. The grass is 15 × 10 − 30 = 120 m².

questions.onCorrect: 120 m². The grass is the whole field minus the cutout.

misconceptions.feedback: 150 m² is the whole field. The pond is not grass.
30 m² is the pond. The grass is the rest.

questions.prompt: A floor is a rectangle with a corner missing. Which finds its area?
hints: Is the missing corner part of the floor?

acceptedIdeas: The whole rectangle's area minus the missing corner's area
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The whole rectangle's area minus the missing corner's area

choices.label: The whole rectangle's area minus the missing corner's area
The whole rectangle's area plus the missing corner's area

questions.onCorrect: Take the missing corner's area from the whole rectangle's area.

misconceptions.feedback: Adding the corner would count floor that isn't there.
Adding sides gives a distance round, not an area.

questions.prompt: Two copies of a trapezoid make one parallelogram. How does one trapezoid's area compare with the parallelogram's?
hints: How many trapezoids make the parallelogram?

acceptedIdeas: It is half
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is half

questions.onCorrect: One trapezoid is half the parallelogram, because two copies make the whole.

misconceptions.feedback: Two trapezoids make the parallelogram, so each one is only part of it.
One trapezoid is only a part of the parallelogram, so it cannot be bigger.

questions.prompt: You walk 3 m east and then 4 m north, a total of 7 m. How does the straight shortcut across compare with the 7 m path?
hints: Which is shorter: the long way round two sides, or straight across?

acceptedIdeas: The shortcut is shorter than 7 m.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The shortcut is the straight line, the shortest route between the two points.

choices.label: The shortcut is shorter than 7 m.
The shortcut is longer than 7 m.

questions.onCorrect: Shorter. A straight line is the shortest route, so it beats the bent path.

misconceptions.feedback: 7 m is the bent path, east then north. A straight line doesn't follow it.
A straight line is the shortest route between two points, so it can't be longer than the bent path.

questions.prompt: Why take the square root at the end?
hints: Is a² + b² a length, or a length squared?

acceptedIdeas: The sum is the square of the hypotenuse, and the root gives its length.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The sum is the square of the hypotenuse, and the root gives its length.

choices.label: The sum is the square of the hypotenuse, and the root gives its length.
Because the answer should be smaller.
Because square roots are always whole numbers.

questions.onCorrect: a² + b² gives c × c. The square root undoes the squaring and gives c itself.

misconceptions.feedback: The root does shrink it, but the reason is that the sum is a square of the length.
Many square roots are not whole numbers. The reason is undoing the squaring.

questions.prompt: A right triangle has legs 8 cm and 15 cm. Find its hypotenuse, in centimetres.
hints: Square each leg.
Add the two squares.
Take the square root of the sum.
questions.onCorrect: 17 cm. 64 + 225 = 289, and the square root of 289 is 17.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the legs. The theorem adds their squares, then takes the square root.
289 is the square of the hypotenuse. Take the square root.

questions.prompt: A right triangle has legs 20 cm and 21 cm. Find its hypotenuse, in centimetres.
hints: Square each leg.
Add the squares: 400 and 441.
Take the square root of the sum.
questions.onCorrect: 29 cm. 400 + 441 = 841, and the square root of 841 is 29.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the legs. The theorem adds their squares first.
841 is the square of the hypotenuse. Take the square root.

questions.prompt: A 10 m ladder leans against a wall with its foot 6 m from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach, in metres?
hints: The ladder is the hypotenuse. What are the legs?
Subtract the square of the known leg from the square of the ladder.
Take the square root of the difference.
questions.onCorrect: 8 m. The ladder is the hypotenuse, so subtract 36 from 100 and take the root.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts the lengths. Subtract the squares, then take the square root.
64 is the square of the height. Take the square root.

questions.prompt: A photo is 4 cm wide and 3 cm tall. It is enlarged so that it is 8 cm wide. How tall should the enlargement be, in centimetres, so the photo isn't stretched?
hints: The width went from 4 cm to 8 cm. How many times bigger is that?
To keep the shape, the height must grow by the same number of times.
Double the 3 cm.
questions.onCorrect: 6 cm. The width doubled, so the height doubles too. Multiplying keeps the shape.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 4 to the height. Adding stretches the photo. The width doubled, so something else must double.
That leaves the height alone, so the photo is stretched sideways.

questions.prompt: Why does the height use the same factor as the width?
hints: What happens to the shape if only the width grows?

acceptedIdeas: Every length in a similar shape is multiplied by the same factor.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every length in a similar shape is multiplied by the same factor.

choices.label: Every length in a similar shape is multiplied by the same factor.
Because height is always bigger than width.
Each side needs its own factor.

questions.onCorrect: Similar shapes use one factor for every length. A different factor would change the shape.

misconceptions.feedback: Either can be bigger. The point is that one factor is shared.
Different factors would stretch the shape out of proportion.

questions.prompt: A triangle has sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm. A similar triangle has a shortest side of 9 cm. Find its longest side, in centimetres.
hints: Match the shortest sides. How many times longer is 9 than 3?
Use that same factor on the longest side.
Multiply 5 by the factor.
questions.onCorrect: 15 cm. Find the factor from one matching pair, then apply it to the other side.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 6 to the longest side. Similar shapes multiply every side by one factor.
That multiplies by 9. Find the factor from the shortest sides first, then use it.

questions.prompt: A 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle is enlarged by scale factor 1.5. What is the new width, in centimetres?
hints: The width is 6 cm. A scale factor multiplies it.
Multiply 6 by 1.5.
Half of 6 is 3. Add that to 6.
questions.onCorrect: 9 cm. Multiply the width by the scale factor: 6 × 1.5.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 1.5 to the width. A scale factor multiplies.
6 cm is the original width. Apply the factor.

questions.prompt: A rectangle is enlarged so its width grows from 4 cm to 12 cm. Its original height was 7 cm. What is the new height, in centimetres?
hints: How many times bigger is the new width than the old?
Use that same factor on the height.
Multiply 7 by the factor.
questions.onCorrect: 21 cm. The factor is 12 ÷ 4 = 3, and the height uses it too.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 8 to the height. Similar shapes multiply every length by one factor.
12 cm is the new width. Find the new height.

questions.prompt: A cube-shaped gift box has sides 3 cm long. It is wrapped in paper with no overlaps. How many square centimetres of paper does it need?
hints: How much paper covers one face?
How many faces does a cube have?
Multiply one face's area by the number of faces.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One face is 3 × 3 = 9 cm². Six faces: 6 × 9 = 54 cm².

questions.onCorrect: 54. One face is 3 × 3 = 9 cm², and a cube has six faces: 6 × 9.

misconceptions.feedback: 9 is one face. A cube has six.
27 counts the cubes inside. Paper covers the outside.

questions.prompt: Why do we double the total of the three face areas?
hints: What sits opposite each face?

acceptedIdeas: Each face has an identical opposite face.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each face has an identical opposite face.

choices.label: Each face has an identical opposite face.
Because the box has two lids.

questions.onCorrect: Faces come in matching opposite pairs, so each of the three areas is counted twice.

misconceptions.feedback: A box has one top and one base. Every face has a matching face opposite it.
Area isn't always doubled. It is the matching pairs of faces that double.

questions.prompt: A closed box measures 6 cm by 4 cm by 1 cm. Find its total surface area in square centimetres.
hints: Find the three different face areas.
Add them, then double.
Faces are 6 × 4, 6 × 1 and 4 × 1.
questions.onCorrect: 68 cm². Add the three different faces, then double the total.

misconceptions.feedback: 34 is the three different faces added once. Double it.
24 is the volume. Surface area adds the face areas.

questions.prompt: A square tile is 2 cm by 2 cm. A bigger copy has every side twice as long. How many of the small tiles would fit inside the big one?
hints: Picture the big tile covered in small tiles. How many fit along one side?
How many rows of that many are there?
Rows times tiles in a row.
questions.onCorrect: 4. Two small tiles fit along each side, and two rows of them: 2 × 2.

misconceptions.feedback: Two fit along one side, but the big tile also has two rows of them.
That counts three directions. A flat tile only has a length and a width.

questions.prompt: Every length of a square is multiplied by 5. By what number is its area multiplied?
hints: The length factor works on the width and on the height.
So it is used twice in the area.
Multiply 5 by 5.
questions.onCorrect: 25. The factor works on both lengths that make up the area: 5 × 5.

misconceptions.feedback: 5 is the length factor. Area uses two lengths, so the factor acts twice.
That adds 5 + 5. The factor multiplies, once in each direction.

questions.prompt: Why is the area multiplied by 3 × 3 and not just 3?
hints: How many lengths does area depend on?

acceptedIdeas: Area multiplies two lengths, and both are multiplied by 3.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Area multiplies two lengths, and both are multiplied by 3.

choices.label: Area multiplies two lengths, and both are multiplied by 3.

questions.onCorrect: Area is length × width. Multiply both by 3 and the area is multiplied by 3 × 3.

misconceptions.feedback: The size of the number doesn't matter. Count how many lengths the area depends on.
Only when every length is tripled. Another factor gives another area factor.

questions.prompt: A shape has area 3 m². A similar copy has every length multiplied by 10. What is the copy's area, in square metres?
hints: The area factor is the length factor used twice.
Work out 10 × 10.
Multiply the area by that.
questions.onCorrect: 300 m². The area factor is 10 × 10 = 100, and 3 × 100 = 300.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by 10 once. Area has two lengths, so use the factor twice.
100 is the area factor. Multiply the original area 3 by it.

questions.prompt: A similar copy has 16 times the area of the original. By what factor were the lengths multiplied?
hints: The area factor is the length factor times itself.
Which number times itself makes 16?
Try a few numbers multiplied by themselves.
questions.onCorrect: 4. The length factor squared is 16, and 4 × 4 = 16.

misconceptions.feedback: That halves 16. Find the number that multiplies by itself to give 16.
That squares 16. Go the other way: which number times itself gives 16?
